sentence: Deep in your skin, right now, a new cell is being born.
claim: New skin cells are produced continuously in the deepest layer of the epidermis (the basal layer, where stem cells divide).
note: [SOURCE-READ via search summary] basal-layer keratinocytes are the proliferative cells of the epidermis. Wording 'right now … being born' is a plain-language version of continuous production. A person opens the source; dermatologist sign-off required.

sentence: It starts at the very bottom… and slowly begins to rise.
claim: Cells made in the basal layer move upward through the epidermis as they differentiate.
note: [SOURCE-READ via search summary] as keratinocytes mature up the epidermis they lose proliferative potential and undergo programmed destruction. A person opens the source; dermatologist sign-off required.

sentence: As it climbs, it fills with a tough protein called keratin. It grows flatter… and flatter.
claim: Keratinocytes produce keratin as they move up and become progressively flatter.
note: [SOURCE-READ via search summary] corneocytes retain keratin filaments in a filaggrin matrix and flatten, stacking as layers; 'a tough protein called keratin' is plain language. A person opens the source; dermatologist sign-off required.

sentence: Near the top, it lets go of its nucleus… and its life gently ends.
claim: In the outer layer the cells lose their nuclei and organelles and become dead, flattened corneocytes.
note: [SOURCE-READ via search summary] finally differentiated, enucleated keratinocytes are termed corneocytes (no nucleus); the cell's end is programmed. A person opens the source; dermatologist sign-off required.

sentence: So the skin you can touch right now is made of cells that have finished their lives.
claim: The outermost layer (stratum corneum) is made of dead corneocytes.
note: [SOURCE-READ via search summary] the outermost layer (stratum corneum) is made of these flattened, enucleated corneocytes. A person opens the source; dermatologist sign-off required.

sentence: Stacked like bricks, they seal in water.
claim: Corneocytes embedded in lipids form a barrier that limits water loss (the bricks-and-mortar model).
source_title: Schmitt & Neubert 2020, review of the stratum corneum barrier (PMC7592940)
note: [SOURCE-READ via search summary] the lipid matrix holds the main penetration barrier; corneocytes are the 'bricks' (Elias 1988 brick-and-mortar model). The model is debated; the film says only that the stack seals water in. She reads 'they seal in water'. A person opens the source; dermatologist sign-off required.

sentence: The whole journey takes about a month.
claim: Epidermal turnover takes roughly a month (about 28 days or more, varying with age and site).
source_title: BioNumbers: turnover time of cells in the entire epidermis (value not read); Iizuka H., J Dermatol Sci 1994;8:215-217 (not opened)
note: [NOT CONFIRMED, RANGE] No primary source was read. Search results (secondary and consumer pages) say: about 28 days is the commonly quoted figure for young adults; a stratum-corneum transit time of roughly 20 days (dansyl chloride tracer) in young adults, over 10 days longer in older adults; and a whole-epidermis estimate of 47–48 days (Iizuka 1994 reanalysis, quoted second-hand) instead of the older 39. So published estimates run from about 3 to about 7 weeks depending on method, age and site; 'about a month' sits inside that range but the whole-epidermis figure may be longer than a month. A person must open Iizuka 1994 and a review before posting. Keep OPEN; decide between keeping the line and re-recording if the source says clearly longer. Textbook figures of about 4 weeks (about 2 weeks rising plus about 2 weeks in the horny layer) sit inside the published range of about 3-7 weeks by method, age and site. IF the opened source gives whole-epidermis transit over 6 weeks, the owner decides between keeping it and Evelyn re-recording 'about a month or more'.

sentence: Then, quietly, the top cells drift away, far too small to see.
claim: The outermost corneocytes are continually shed (desquamation) as microscopic flakes.
note: [SOURCE-READ via search summary] cells are shed (desquamate) when adhesion between corneocytes weakens. A person opens the source; dermatologist sign-off required.

sentence: Some of the dust in your home… began as you.
claim: Skin scales (desquamated skin) are a real component of the particles in room air and dust; the share varies widely, and 'most dust is skin' is not supported.
source_title: Clark RP, Skin scales among airborne particles, J Hyg (Lond) 1974;72:47-51 (PMC2130262; PubMed 4522246)
note: [SOURCE-READ via search summary, abstract level] microscopy showed many airborne particles in rooms, and some from outside air, appear to be scales of desquamated skin, with protein in many of them. No fraction is given; popular '70–80% of dust is skin' figures are not supported, so the line says only 'some of the dust'. A person should open the paper (and a household-dust study such as the Weschler group's 2011 work on skin flakes) before posting.

sentence: Underneath, new cells are already rising. Always rebuilding… from the bottom up.
claim: The epidermis renews itself continuously from the basal layer.
note: [SOURCE-READ via search summary] basal keratinocytes keep producing new cells that move up. A person opens the source; dermatologist sign-off required.
